sources.name: URMA (Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis), NOAA
sources.description: NOAA's hourly analysis of weather near the ground on a 2.5 km grid, which combines weather station observations with a short forecast. It is published about 6 hours after the hour.

sources.name: URMA (Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis), NOAA
sources.description: URMA's hourly precipitation, from radar and rain gauges, from the day it began.

sources.name: RTMA (Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis), NOAA
sources.description: Before URMA published hourly precipitation, its real-time counterpart RTMA did, so the archive's hourly precipitation comes from RTMA until then.

sources.name: RTMA (Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis), NOAA
sources.description: RTMA is published about an hour after the hour. It fills the newest hours until URMA's arrive and replace them.

sources.name: HRRR (High-Resolution Rapid Refresh), NOAA
sources.description: Solar radiation from NOAA's hourly weather model on its 3 km grid, taken to our grid, as the mean of each hour's four 15-minute values (in 2016, values at each quarter hour rather than means over it), and corrected to pyranometers on the ground.

sources.name: ERA5-Land, ECMWF (Copernicus Climate Change Service)
sources.description: ECMWF's reanalysis of the land surface on a 9 km grid, taken to our grid: soil temperature at each depth, and soil moisture as the water in each of the model's soil layers. It is published about 5 days behind.

sources.name: ECMWF IFS (Integrated Forecasting System), through Open-Meteo
sources.description: ECMWF's forecast model fills soil temperature, soil moisture and snow depth for the days since ERA5-Land's last, its soil adjusted to meet ERA5-Land's, until ERA5-Land's values arrive and replace them.

sources.name: NBM (National Blend of Models), NOAA
sources.description: NOAA's forecast blended from many weather models, on the same 2.5 km grid, for the next 11 days. We correct its daily highs, overnight lows, humidity and solar radiation against the archive.

sources.name: ECMWF IFS (Integrated Forecasting System), through Open-Meteo
sources.description: Soil temperature, soil moisture and snow depth in the forecast, the soil adjusted to meet the archive's.

sources.name: Open-Meteo
sources.description: For locations outside the area our maps cover, and for dates before our archive, we read weather for the location from Open-Meteo: NBM where it has it, then its best match of weather models, with ERA5 and ERA5-Land for earlier years and ECMWF IFS for soil and snow. We correct its solar radiation and humidity against Wisconsin's stations and the archive. If our own forecast hasn't been updated for more than 12 hours, the forecast for a location inside our area comes from Open-Meteo too until ours is current again; our maps show no forecast meanwhile.

sources.name: gridMET, Climatology Lab
sources.description: A gridded daily weather dataset on a 4 km grid. The 30-year normal takes from it the years before our archive begins, adjusted to the archive cell by cell.

corrections.title: Solar radiation in the archive
corrections.summary: The HRRR model's solar radiation reads about 18% high against pyranometers on the ground. We correct each hour by a factor that depends on how clear the hour was (HRRR's radiation as a share of the radiation on a clear day), fitted against 80 Wisconet pyranometers in 2025 and tested on 2026. Reference evapotranspiration and daily totals are computed from the corrected values, and we keep HRRR's own values too.

scores.measure: Daily total, ratio to the stations'

corrections.title: Solar radiation in the forecast
corrections.summary: The National Blend of Models (NBM) forecasts too little solar radiation on days it expects to be very cloudy and too much on days it expects to be clear, more so the further ahead the day is, and about 11% too much overall. We correct each forecast hour by a factor that depends on how far ahead the day is and how clear NBM expects it to be, fitted against the archive's corrected radiation for 73 forecasts made in 2025.

scores.measure: Daily total, ratio to the archive's, days 1 to 10
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

scores.measure: Daily total on day 1, mean absolute error
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

corrections.title: Daily highs in the forecast
corrections.summary: NBM's hourly temperatures and its own forecast of the day's high don't always agree. We reshape each day's warm hours to reach NBM's forecast high, less a small seasonal offset (−0.4 to +0.6 °C) fitted against the archive's daily highs in 2025.

scores.measure: Daily high on day 3, mean difference from the archive
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

corrections.title: Overnight lows in the forecast
corrections.summary: NBM's hourly temperatures run warm at night, by about 0.5 °C on the first night and up to 1.9 °C a week or more ahead. We lower each night's coldest hours (6 p.m. to 6 a.m. CST) by that warm bias for how far ahead the night is, fitted against the archive's daily lows in 2025.

scores.measure: Daily low on day 1, mean difference from the archive
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

scores.measure: Daily low on day 10, mean difference from the archive
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

corrections.title: Humidity in the forecast
corrections.summary: NBM forecasts fewer humid hours than the archive records. We map each forecast hour's relative humidity onto the archive's, by season, hour of the day and how far ahead it is, and compute the dew point from it, keeping the temperature. Disease models that count humid hours read the result.

scores.measure: Hours a day with humidity at or above 80% on day 1, mean difference from the archive
scores.tested: 2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others
2025, each forecast tested on a fit to the others

corrections.title: Soil temperature and moisture on the newest days and in the forecast
corrections.summary: Our soil temperature and moisture come from ERA5-Land, which arrives about five days late. ECMWF's forecast model (IFS) fills the days since and the forecast. The two differ (IFS's soil is colder in winter and drier most of the year), so we shift each cell's IFS values by the difference between them at ERA5-Land's last hour, by less and less the further ahead the hour is. ERA5-Land replaces these values when it arrives.

scores.measure: Soil at 4 cm, 3 days ahead, root mean square difference from ERA5-Land
Soil at 10 cm, 3 days ahead, root mean square difference from ERA5-Land
Soil moisture, 0 to 7 cm, 3 days ahead, root mean square difference from ERA5-Land
Soil moisture, 7 to 28 cm, 3 days ahead, root mean square difference from ERA5-Land

corrections.title: Solar radiation outside our area
corrections.summary: For locations outside the area our maps cover, and for dates before our archive, we read weather from Open-Meteo. Its solar radiation reads high against pyranometers, so we correct it the way we correct the archive's, by how clear each hour was, fitted against 80 Wisconet pyranometers. The fit is from Wisconsin, and we apply it everywhere until we can check it against stations elsewhere.

scores.measure: Daily total, ratio to the stations'

corrections.title: Humidity outside our area
corrections.summary: Open-Meteo's humidity gives fewer humid hours than our archive and the stations. We map each hour's relative humidity onto the archive's, by season and hour of the day, and compute the dew point from it, keeping the temperature, so disease models outside our area read humidity like the archive's. It closes about half of the gap; Open-Meteo's humidity also changes from year to year. We apply it only in the Upper Midwest, where it was fitted: at five Oklahoma stations it made spring several times too humid, so farther south we use Open-Meteo's humidity as it comes.

scores.measure: Hours a day with humidity at or above 90%, May to September (stations: 7.54)

corrections.title: Humid hours for disease models
corrections.summary: Several disease models count hours with relative humidity at or above 90%, as measured at a field weather station. Gridded humidity is an average over a 2.5 km cell, so it reaches 90% less often than a station does. We count those hours at 88% instead, the threshold at which the archive has as many humid hours as 80 Wisconet stations and as many as their leaf wetness sensors, May to September 2025 and 2026. Open-Meteo's humidity, which we use outside our area, matched five Oklahoma Mesonet stations' hours at 90% at about the same threshold, 88%, from March to August 2023 to 2025, so pecan scab's hours are counted the same way.

corrections.title: The earlier years of the 30-year normal
corrections.summary: Our archive begins in 2016, so the 30-year normal takes its earlier years from gridMET, a gridded daily weather dataset (Abatzoglou, 2013). The two differ: gridMET's daily highs, for one, run about 0.7 °F warmer than the archive's over the years both cover. We adjust gridMET to the archive cell by cell and day of the year, by the difference (temperature, humidity) or the ratio (precipitation, solar radiation, wind, evapotranspiration) between them, so the normal's years are on one basis. We leave out gridMET's daily highs and evapotranspiration for 2011–2013, which run 3–6 °F warm in summer against every station we checked.
